params.note: An original beat on the 909 kit, played at full quality, then resampled at the SP-1200's 26.04 kHz and 12 bits with each sample held and no smoothing afterwards (Wikipedia, E-mu SP-1200: the reconstruction filter was deliberately omitted). A crusher worklet, not a model of the machine's converters or its analog filters.

caption.age7: Switch it on and the drums get a little bit crunchy at the top.
caption.age13: Switch to B and listen to the hi-hats. The SP-1200 stored sound as 12-bit numbers, 26,040 times a second, and its makers left out the filter that would have smoothed the result. That puts a slight crunchy edge on the top of everything, and hip-hop producers wanted it.
caption.adult: B resamples the loop at the SP-1200's rate and resolution and holds each sample with no reconstruction filter, so images above the Nyquist frequency brighten the top end. The difference is meant to be small: it is the slight crunch the machine is known for, not a lo-fi effect. The other half of the machine's story, ten seconds of sampling time, cannot be heard in a loop this short.
